subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: The brain and behaviour: localization, neuroplasticity, neurotransmitters
Hormones and pheromones and their effects on behaviour
The relationship between genetics and behaviour
Ethical considerations and research methods in the biological approach

questions.q: Maguire et al. (2000) found that London taxi drivers had a larger posterior hippocampus than controls. This is most often used as evidence of:
options: The effect of neurotransmitters on memory
questions.explain: Years of navigational experience were associated with structural change in the hippocampus, illustrating neuroplasticity.

questions.q: In Sperry's split-brain studies, an object presented only to the LEFT visual field could not be verbally named because:
options: The information reached the right hemisphere, which lacks the dominant language centres, and the severed corpus callosum blocked transfer
The left hemisphere was damaged in these patients
The object was processed by the cerebellum
Split-brain patients are unable to see the left visual field
questions.explain: The left visual field projects to the right hemisphere; with the corpus callosum cut, that information cannot reach the language-dominant left hemisphere to be named.

questions.q: The patient HM, studied by Milner, developed severe anterograde amnesia after surgical removal of tissue in the:
options: Medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus
questions.explain: Bilateral removal of medial temporal lobe structures, including the hippocampus, left HM unable to form new long-term declarative memories.

questions.q: Rosenzweig and Bennett found that rats raised in enriched environments developed a thicker cerebral cortex than those in impoverished conditions. This supports the idea that:
options: Environmental stimulation can produce measurable changes in brain structure
Brain structure is fixed at birth
Neurotransmitter levels are unaffected by experience
questions.explain: Enrichment increased dendritic branching and cortical thickness, evidence of environmentally driven neuroplasticity.

questions.q: Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter that has been particularly implicated in:
questions.explain: Acetylcholine plays a key role in memory; for example, Rogers and Kesner linked it to encoding in the hippocampus.

questions.q: A researcher uses fMRI to show amygdala activation while participants view fearful faces. A strength of fMRI here is that it:
options: Provides good spatial resolution of active brain areas non-invasively
Establishes that the amygdala causes fear
questions.explain: fMRI shows where activity occurs with good spatial detail, but because nothing is manipulated it shows correlation, not causation.

questions.q: Cortisol, a hormone involved in the body's stress response, is released by the:
questions.explain: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid secreted by the adrenal cortex as part of the HPA axis stress response.

questions.q: Newcomer et al. (1999) found participants given high doses of cortisol performed worse on a verbal declarative memory task. This suggests that prolonged high cortisol:
questions.explain: Elevated cortisol was associated with poorer declarative memory, indicating a disruptive effect on hippocampal memory processes.

questions.q: Oxytocin is most commonly associated with which class of behaviour?
questions.explain: Studies such as Baumgartner et al. link oxytocin to trust and affiliative behaviour, though effects are context-dependent.

questions.q: Compared with the evidence for hormones, the evidence that human PHEROMONES influence behaviour is best described as:
questions.explain: Putative human pheromone effects (e.g. androstadienone studies) remain contested and inconsistent, unlike well-supported hormone effects.

questions.q: A study reports that intranasal oxytocin increased trusting behaviour in an investment game. A cautious conclusion is that oxytocin:
options: May modulate social behaviour, but effects depend on context and replication is mixed
Directly and reliably causes trust in all situations
Has been proven to eliminate distrust
questions.explain: Single-study effects should be interpreted cautiously; oxytocin research shows context dependence and variable replication.

questions.q: Twin studies estimate the genetic contribution to a behaviour by comparing concordance rates between:
questions.explain: MZ twins share ~100% of genes and DZ ~50%; a higher MZ concordance suggests a genetic contribution.

questions.q: Caspi et al. (2003) found that a variant of the 5-HTT (serotonin transporter) gene predicted depression only among people who had experienced stressful life events. This illustrates:
options: That genes have no role in depression
questions.explain: The gene's effect on depression depended on environmental stress, a classic gene-environment (GxE) interaction.

questions.q: A trait shows 70% concordance in MZ twins and 30% in DZ twins. The most accurate interpretation is that the trait:
options: Has a genetic component but is also influenced by the environment
Is entirely determined by the environment
questions.explain: Higher MZ than DZ concordance implies genetic influence, but concordance below 100% shows the environment also contributes.

questions.q: A limitation of using family studies to argue that depression is genetic is that:
options: Relatives usually share environments as well as genes
Depression is not heritable at all
questions.explain: Shared family environment is confounded with shared genes, so family aggregation alone cannot isolate genetic causes.

questions.q: Studies correlating brain structure with a behaviour using MRI cannot establish cause and effect mainly because:
questions.explain: Correlational imaging observes associations without manipulation, so direction of causation cannot be determined.

questions.q: Informed consent, the right to withdraw and protection from harm are examples of:
options: Ethical considerations that apply to research with human participants
questions.explain: These are core ethical requirements protecting participants in psychological research.

questions.q: A researcher wants strong evidence that a drug that raises serotonin reduces aggression. The most appropriate design would be:
options: A controlled experiment manipulating the drug with a placebo comparison
questions.explain: Only a controlled experiment with manipulation and a comparison group can support a causal claim about the drug's effect.

questions.q: When a study uses brain imaging, a methodological strength is objectivity, but a common weakness is that:
options: Findings are often correlational and may not reflect real-world behaviour
questions.explain: Imaging is objective and replicable but typically correlational and conducted in artificial settings, limiting ecological validity and causal claims.

questions.q: A neurotransmitter agonist is a substance that:
options: Increases or mimics the action of a neurotransmitter
questions.explain: Agonists enhance or imitate a neurotransmitter's effect, whereas antagonists block it.

questions.q: Adrenaline (epinephrine), released during the fight-or-flight response, prepares the body by:
options: Increasing heart rate and mobilising energy
Slowing all body systems to rest
questions.explain: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla rapidly raises heart rate, blood flow and energy availability for action.

questions.q: A heritability estimate indicates the proportion of the variation in a trait within a population that is attributable to:
questions.explain: Heritability describes how much of the observed variation in a population is linked to genetic variation, not the cause in one person.
